method.method_draft: Use fixed seat indexing and rotate the final circular order. First read the diagram as five fixed table positions clockwise: A at the top, then B at upper right, C at lower right, D at lower left, and E at upper left. Label these positions 0 through 4, initially occupied by A,B,C,D,E. From the text, the final clockwise order is A,E,B,D,C, but because the table is round this order may start at any fixed position, so test its five rotations as assignments to positions 0-4. For each rotation, check which kangaroos stayed in the same numbered position and whether every other kangaroo moved exactly one position clockwise or counterclockwise. The only rotation that works is positions 0-4 = E,B,D,C,A, which is the same circular order as A,E,B,D,C. In that arrangement, B remains at position 1, while A and E swap neighboring seats and C and D swap neighboring seats. Therefore B did not change places.

method.method_draft: Use the forced-pair-swap structure created by one stationary kangaroo. Read from the diagram that the initial clockwise cycle is A-B-C-D-E. From the text, exactly one kangaroo stays put and every other kangaroo moves to an adjacent seat. Try each possible stationary kangaroo conceptually: if a kangaroo stays in its seat, the four remaining seats form two forced adjacent swaps, because the two seats next to the fixed kangaroo cannot move into the occupied fixed seat and must move to their other neighbor. For example, if B is fixed, then on one side C and D must swap, and on the other side A and E must swap. This produces the clockwise seating E,B,D,C,A, which is the same circular order as A,E,B,D,C. The other choices of fixed kangaroo produce different circular orders, so the fixed kangaroo is B.
